column3: Dense bucket array sized by the read's own half-length, not the reference
column4: Peak memory; incidentally fixed a multithreading speed bug (§1)
column5: ~4 MB/worker vs the C++'s constant ~15 GB — the 6.9-7.4x-less-memory headline (RESULTS.md §1) is almost entirely this. On a 6,000-read whole-genome run: `bucket_merge` 1342.1 s → 39.1 s, whole run 1995.6 s → 725.6 s
column6: Yes — byte-identical output; the dense and sparse-fallback paths are tested to agree exactly

column3: Streaming multi-hit seeds — no per-seed scratch hashmap
column5: Not isolated as its own standalone percentage in the record; replaces ~O(hits) hashmap inserts with O(1) integer work per hit (§2)
column6: Yes — same buckets receive the same accumulated, clamped content

column3: `RefineCache` — the second-best search replays the first's scores instead of recomputing them
column5: 44% of `find_best_mapping` calls eliminated, flat across 1x/3x/10x coverage: `match_rest_for_best2` **-66 to -67%**, `refine` **-39 to -41%**, `query_mapping` **-9 to -11%** (§3)
column6: Yes — byte-identical PAF; restricted to exactly the two metrics (Containment, Jaccard) where it's provably safe — **not** applied to `bucket_SH`/`bucket_LCS`

column3: Final bucket ordering: an unstable sort on a packed key reproduces stable-sort output — the paper's own Algorithm 4 "Optimization 2"
column4: Sort cost in `get_sorted_buckets`, and (as a side effect) determinism
column5: Sorts 8-byte packed keys instead of 32-byte records — no isolated standalone percentage in the record, but real: moving 4x fewer bytes and skipping a stable sort's temporary allocation
column6: Yes, and stronger than the C++: reproduces exactly what a *stable* sort by descending match count would give (the original index is packed in as the tiebreak), where the C++'s `std::sort` gives no such guarantee even between its own runs (`src/buckets.rs`'s `get_sorted_buckets` doc comment)

column3: Multithreaded read mapping — a capability, not present in the C++ at all
column5: RESULTS.md §2 (single-thread and `-@4` per benchmark) and §3 (the full thread-scaling table, including the NUMA ceiling Q4/Q5 diagnosed)
column6: Yes — byte-identical regardless of thread count (`tests/multithreaded_parity.rs`)

column3: Hash-sharded index storage + chunked reference sketching, both parallel across `-@`
column5: `index_initializing` **8.4 s → 1.1-1.8 s**; chunked sketching **~18% off `indexing`** at `-@8` (§5)
column6: Yes — index contents never depend on thread count

column4: Indexing wall time (the reading phase specifically) + peak RSS
column6: Yes — `debug_assert`-pinned: pass 2 writes exactly what pass 1 counted, with no gaps

column3: Sketching/index hot loop: precomputed rotation tables, bounds-check-free iteration, `Entry` API, binomial-sized sketch buffers
column5: **~13-17% off `index_sketching`** is the bounds-check-free iteration alone (§7); the other three items in this row have no isolated standalone percentage in the record

column3: Lower allocation/memory traffic: `PMatches` inline for the common single-occurrence case, `Match` borrows its `Seed`, dense `diff_hist`, no `seq` field on `RefSegment`, FASTA records by value, bounded read-ahead, buffered stdout, `lto="fat"`
column4: Peak memory, and speed via fewer allocations
column5: **~11-13% off peak RSS** is the bounded read-ahead alone; **~5% wall** is `lto="fat"` alone (§8); the rest are allocation-*count* reductions (e.g. ~300 M fewer heap allocations for single-occurrence seeds) without an isolated standalone percentage in the record
